name: Tuva
summary_text: The Republic of Tyva (Tuva) stands under the national framework of Russia, and the source inventory contains no division-specific transgender evidence for this republic. A trans visitor to Tuva is therefore assessed against the countrywide regime as it operates there.  Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition are banned: the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender changes on official documents was signed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court of Russia designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.  The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework this republic is assessed against. It records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, that 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and that the note carries no information specific to Tuva beyond the national framework. The same Home Office policy affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims.  Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. It also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. That article carries no Tuva-specific detail; it sets the national enforcement baseline against which Tuva is scored, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.  Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.  Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. In July 2024 the BBC followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

name: Udmurtia
summary_text: Udmurtia has produced no division-specific transgender evidence in the available sources. A visitor to the republic of Udmurtia stands under the national framework of Russia as it operates countrywide, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework against which this division is assessed.  Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the UK Home Office note records that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in November 2023.  The expanded 'propaganda' statute criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.  Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia, with 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reaching up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.  Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.  Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.  Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.  The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

sources.title: Federal law on 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual relationships' (2013, expanded 2022)
sources.documents: National legal status criminalizing distribution of materials promoting non-traditional relationships and gender transition; applies in Udmurtia as federal law
sources.detail: Cited as passed 2013 criminalising distribution among minors; expanded 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age and to prohibit materials that make minors interested in gender transitions
